title: Day 1 · Phase 1 — Re-anchoring: what makes 2026-XJ move?
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · Phase 1 — Setting up the question

You predicted WHERE 2026-XJ is going. Today we start asking WHY.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS (preview)

K1. Universal gravitation as the force that runs the asteroid show. R4. Why 2026-XJ doesn't drift away.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model.

How today connects:

end of Unit 1, students have a velocity-time prediction for the asteroid based on radar data.

Today's pivot: Unit 1 answered "how fast?" Unit 2 answers "why fast?" — which is the same as "what force?" The unit's load-bearing question is whether 2026-XJ's path bends enough to bring it to Earth.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Return Unit 1 transfer tasks. Highlight one or two strong predictions. Reframe: "Your prediction assumed velocity stays constant. It doesn't. Why?"

5–18 min

• Demo: drop a hardcover book + a flat sheet of paper at the same height, same release. Then crumple the paper, repeat. Ask the room: "Why did the rule change?" Lead to: without air resistance, all objects fall the same.

18–28 min

• Notice & Wonder — students list what they notice about the demo, what they wonder about gravity. Sort into "physics can answer" / "physics cannot answer."

28–42 min

• Mini-lecture preview: gravity is a force, and it follows a law (Newton's universal gravitation). Don't derive it yet — frame the unit's question: "Knowing the law, we can predict whether 2026-XJ's orbit bends toward us."

42–48 min

• Individual exit: Why doesn't 2026-XJ just drift off into space at constant velocity? What pulls on it?

48–50 min

• Marzano conversation on K1/R4 preview.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Listen for gravity as an interaction that changes velocity. Compare the flat-paper and crumpled-paper predictions: students must distinguish air resistance from gravitational acceleration.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Unit 1 transfer tasks scored; hardcover book + sheet of paper; clear floor zone; whiteboard with two columns ("physics can answer" / "can't").

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 13 §13.1–13.2.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §6.5 Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation (pp. 261–264). Focus: Introduce universal gravitation as the interaction that can change an asteroid's velocity; distinguish it from inertia. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the demo: resist the temptation to explain. Push the room: "What's the same about the book and the crumpled paper that's different about the flat paper?" Let air resistance surface from them.

Differentiation: ELs — sentence frames for the exit ticket; SWDs — written prompt + a verbal version offered; Honors extension — ask "if there's NO air on a different planet, what's the equivalent demo?"

Online sequence: save the drop-race prediction, run or watch the trials, record an observation and revision, then open the explanation. A curiosity question is optional, not the main evidence.

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 2 · Phase 2 — Free fall: everything falls at g
bodyHtml:
DAY 2 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

g = 9.81 m/s² near Earth. Why every object — coin, feather, asteroid — accelerates the same.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K1. Gravity as a constant acceleration near Earth. S4. Reading g off a v-t slope.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Re-anchoring: what makes 2026-XJ move?.

How today connects:

Near Earth's surface, its gravitational acceleration is approximately g; at larger distances the field strength changes with distance from Earth's center. We need to know what g is — and that it's the SAME for the asteroid as for a coin you drop.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick read-back of best Day-1 exit tickets. Anchor: "Ignoring air resistance, objects near the same location have the same gravitational acceleration; their gravitational forces depend on mass." Bring receipts.

5–18 min

• Vernier motion detector demo: drop a ball, project the v-t graph. Slope = g. Repeat with a different ball — slope is the same.

18–32 min

• Worked examples on the board: How long to fall 10 m from rest? 100 m? Use v = gt and y = ½gt². Two examples fully worked.

32–45 min

• Pair practice — 4 problems on the packet. Predict-then-check using a stopwatch + drop (when safe).

45–48 min

• Exit ticket: "How long does it take a coin to fall 1 m from rest, ignoring air?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that the velocity–time slope has units m/s² and that equal acceleration does not mean equal gravitational force on different masses.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Vernier motion detector + ball; tape measure; stopwatch for student trials; packet pages.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 4 §4.5. Honors: Ch 4 §4.5–4.6 + Think and Solve 52, 53, 56; Ch 6 §6.6.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §2.7 Falling Objects (pp. 75–80). Focus: Set a positive direction for free fall and state the near-Earth, negligible-air-resistance assumptions. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: after the v-t demo, "What does the slope mean physically? What would a STEEPER slope tell you?"

Differentiation: ELs — pair a calculator-fluent partner with a language partner; Honors extension — "what would g be on a planet with twice Earth's mass at the same radius?" (preview Day 6).

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 3 · Phase 2 — Weight as F = mg (local gravity)
bodyHtml:
DAY 3 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

F = mg works HERE because g is local. The asteroid's weight on Earth ≠ its weight at lunar distance.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K2. Weight vs. mass; gravitational field strength as a local quantity.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Free fall: everything falls at g.

How today connects:

If we put 2026-XJ on a giant scale on Earth's surface, what would it read? Set up the question — answer it after we have F = Gm₁m₂/r² in hand on Day 4.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: "What's your mass? What's your weight on Earth? On the Moon? On 2026-XJ?" Get class to articulate that one of these is the SAME everywhere.

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: mass is how much stuff (kg, universal). Weight is the force of gravity ON that mass (N, depends on local g). F = mg.

18–32 min

• Worked example progression: 70-kg student on Earth (g=9.81), Moon (g=1.62), Mars (g=3.71), asteroid surface (g≈0.0003). Pattern emerges: mass constant, weight scales with g.

32–45 min

• Independent practice — 6 problems on a worksheet. Mix masses, mix g values. Aspen-style answer column.

45–48 min

• Exit ticket: "If you weigh 600 N on Earth, what is your mass? What would you weigh on a planet with g = 25 m/s²?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K2. Tomorrow: where does g COME FROM?

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check for kilograms on mass and newtons on weight. A successful comparison keeps mass fixed and changes the local gravitational field strength.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: worksheet printed; calculators if needed; small bathroom scale as a prop ("this measures FORCE, not mass").

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 3 §3.5. Honors: Ch 3 §3.5 + Think and Solve 51, 53; Ch 13 §13.8.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §4.3 Newton’s Second Law of Motion: Concept of a System (pp. 161–166). Focus: Focus on Mass and Weight. Distinguish kilograms from newtons and explain why weight depends on the local gravitational field. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: when students conflate mass and weight, push back: "You just said you'd weigh less on the Moon. Did your mass change? What did?"

Differentiation: ELs — cognate pair (masa / mass; peso / weight) on the board, refer often; SWDs — a 3-column table (planet | g | weight) to organize work; Honors extension — "derive Mars g from Mars's mass and radius" (preview Day 6).

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

title: Day 4 · Phase 2 — Newton's law of universal gravitation
bodyHtml:
DAY 4 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

F = G m₁ m₂ / r². Every mass pulls every other mass.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K1. Universal gravitation as an inverse-square law. R1. Reasoning about how F changes with mass and distance (preview).

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Weight as F = mg (local gravity).

How today connects:

This is THE equation we've been building toward. Every distance the asteroid moves changes the force on it. The 1/r² geometry decides how steeply the force ramps up as it approaches.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–3 min

• Quick check: "What's mass? What's weight? Why did weight change on Mars yesterday?"

3–18 min

• Direct instruction: F = G m₁ m₂ / r². Walk through each piece. G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ (tiny — why gravity is the weakest force at human scales). The 1/r² geometry — surface of a sphere grows as r².

18–32 min

• PhET Gravity Force Lab. Vary m₁, m₂, r. Students predict-then-check: "If I double m₁, what happens to F?" "If I double r?" "Triple r?"

32–42 min

• Worked example on the board: F between Earth (6×10²⁴ kg) and a 1000-kg asteroid at 384,000 km. Get to a number, name it, contextualize it.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "If 2026-XJ doubles its distance from Earth, what happens to F_gravity? Triples?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1. Tomorrow: calculation day.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for a factor of one quarter when separation doubles, with the masses held fixed. If students halve the force, return to the squared-distance comparison.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: PhET Gravity Force Lab loaded on lab computers; copy of the inverse-square diagram (concentric spheres) for the board.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 13 §13.4. Honors: Ch 13 §13.1–13.4 + Think and Solve 57, 60.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §6.5 Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation (pp. 261–266). Focus: Identify the two masses and center-to-center separation; explain the inverse-square relation before calculating. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: when students reach for "twice the distance, twice the change in force" — push: "Look at the EXPONENT. What does squared mean here?"

Differentiation: ELs — write the equation with words above each symbol; SWDs — pre-built table for the PhET activity; Honors extension — "if Earth's mass were halved AND distance doubled, what happens to F? Reason BEFORE you compute."

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 5 · Phase 2 — F = Gm₁m₂/r² calculation day
bodyHtml:
DAY 5 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Run the numbers. Build the intuition through repetition with variation.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S1. Computing F = Gm₁m₂/r². R1. Reasoning about how F scales with each input.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Newton's law of universal gravitation.

How today connects:

Students compute F for the actual Earth/Sun/Moon/2026-XJ combinations. Pattern: gravity dominates between BIG things at SHORT distances.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick recap of Day 4: G value, equation, the 1/r² geometry.

5–18 min

• Group worked example: Earth–Moon force at average separation. Get the number. "Is this big? Compare to your weight." (it's enormous)

18–35 min

• Group rotation: 5 problems, 4 minutes each. Mix Earth–Moon, Earth–Sun, Moon–Sun, Earth–asteroid at different separations. Each station has a calculator and the equation visible.

35–43 min

• Class compiles a table on the board: pair, separation, force. Pattern-finding: which pair gives the BIGGEST F? Which changes most when r doubles?

43–48 min

• Exit ticket: "If the asteroid is currently at 5 lunar distances from Earth, and it gets to 1 lunar distance, how many times larger is the force?" (Answer: 25×.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on S1, R1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check center-to-center distance, SI units, and the square on the entire distance. Ask students to predict the direction of change before accepting a calculator result.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: 5 station problem cards with masses + distances; calculators; whiteboard space for the class compilation.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 13 §13.5. Honors: Ch 13 §13.5 + Think and Solve 58, 59, 61, 62.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §6.5 Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation (pp. 261–266). Focus: Work through the gravitation examples with scientific notation and units; compare ratio reasoning with direct substitution. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: after the Earth–Moon calculation, "This number is huge. So why don't we feel it pulling US into the Moon?" (Push toward: the force is on Earth as a whole, and we're in orbit with Earth.)

Differentiation: ELs — give the equation with all masses, distances, and G pre-labeled; SWDs — fewer stations, more time at each; Honors extension — "what's the F between two students sitting 1 m apart?" (Tiny — point: gravity is weak at small mass.)

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. title: Day 6 · Phase 2 — Gravitational fields — g as field strength
bodyHtml:
DAY 6 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

g = GM/r². The local gravitational field at any distance from a mass.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K2. Gravitational field as F per unit mass; g = GM/r².

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on F = Gm₁m₂/r² calculation day.

How today connects:

Earth makes a gravitational field everywhere in space. As 2026-XJ moves through that field, the force it feels changes. The field is the bridge between "Earth's mass" and "force on the asteroid."

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap Day 5: F = Gm₁m₂/r².

5–15 min

• The field move: divide both sides of F = Gm₁m₂/r² by m_test. Define g(r) = GM/r² — the gravitational field strength at distance r from a mass M. Units: N/kg or m/s² (they're the same).

15–28 min

• Worked examples: g at Earth's surface (r = 6.37×10⁶ m, M = 6×10²⁴) — should be 9.8. g at ISS altitude (r = 6.77×10⁶ m). g at the Moon's orbit. g at the asteroid's current distance.

28–40 min

• Class table: altitude, g. Pattern: g(r) drops as 1/r². Half-strength altitude. 1%-strength altitude.

40–48 min

• Conceptual exit ticket: "Why is the ISS NOT 'in zero gravity' even though astronauts float?" (Answer: g there ≈ 8.7 m/s². They float because the ISS is in free fall AROUND Earth.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on K2.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for g = F/m in N/kg and its equivalence to m/s². Students should explain orbital weightlessness as shared free fall, not absence of gravity.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Table template for the altitude–g compilation; calculator availability; a quick "floating astronaut" image to puncture the misconception.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 13 §13.6. Honors: Ch 13 §13.6–13.7 + Think and Solve 53, 55.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §6.5 Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation (pp. 264–268). Focus: Connect gravitational force per unit mass to field strength. Use the course notes to represent the field with arrows. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves: when a student says "there's no gravity in space" — DON'T correct immediately. Ask: "What's the value of g at the ISS altitude? Compute it. Now is that zero?" Let the math do the work.

Differentiation: ELs — visual of concentric spheres around Earth with g written on each; SWDs — pre-tabled altitude/g rows to fill; Honors extension — "derive Mars's g from M_Mars and r_Mars," then compare.

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 7 · Phase 2 — g varies with altitude — preview to orbits
bodyHtml:
DAY 7 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Graphing g vs. altitude. Setting up the orbit conversation that closes the unit.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K2. g(r) qualitatively + graphically. R3. Comparing g across distances and bodies.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Gravitational fields — g as field strength.

How today connects:

The asteroid's distance is changing. So is g where it is. We can't use 9.81 m/s² for an asteroid that's a million kilometers from Earth — but we CAN use g(r) = GM/r².

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–3 min

• Quick recap: g = GM/r². Units: N/kg.

3–18 min

• Graph activity: Plot g vs. altitude (above Earth surface). Use Desmos or a worksheet grid. 5 points: surface, 100 km, 1000 km, 10000 km, lunar distance. Connect the curve.

18–30 min

• Reading the graph: where does g drop to half? To 10%? To 1%? Connect altitude to physical meaning (LEO, GEO, moon orbit).

30–42 min

• Bridge: weightlessness. ISS astronauts experience g ≈ 8.7 m/s². They float because they're FALLING. Free fall + horizontal motion = orbit. This is Day 13's argument; plant the seed now.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "At what altitude does Earth's g drop to half its surface value?" (Answer: r where GM/r² = 4.9, so r ≈ √(GM/4.9) = ~9×10⁶ m, or ~2500 km altitude.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on K2/R3. Tomorrow: measure g in the lab.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that the horizontal variable is distance from Earth's center, not altitude alone. The graph decreases toward zero without reaching zero at a finite distance.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Graph templates or Desmos pre-loaded on lab computers; an ISS image to anchor the orbit preview.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 13 §13.8 + Think and Solve 56, 63, 64; Ch 14 §14.1.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §6.5 Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation (pp. 264–268). Focus: Replace altitude with distance from Earth's center and explain why g changes with location. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on weightlessness: Push hard on the misconception. "If the ISS were ACTUALLY in zero gravity, what would happen to it? Would it stay in orbit?" The answer (it'd fly off in a straight line) sets up Newton's cannon on Day 13.

Differentiation: ELs — provide the graph axes pre-labeled with units; SWDs — partner up for the graph; Honors extension — "what altitude gives g = g_Moon (1.62)?"

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

title: Day 8 · Phase 2 — Vernier free-fall lab: measure g
bodyHtml:
DAY 8 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Vernier motion detector + ball drop. Capture v-t. Compute g from slope. Compare to 9.81.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S4. Use a Vernier motion detector to measure g. K1. Consolidate.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on g varies with altitude — preview to orbits.

How today connects:

We've been using g = 9.81 m/s² for a week. Today we MEASURE it. If the lab number matches theory, the F = Gm₁m₂/r² framework we're using for 2026-XJ is on solid ground.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Lab procedure overview + safety beat (ball drop, watch heads + feet, clear floor zone).

5–15 min

• Demo run by teacher: motion detector pointed up, ball dropped above it, v-t graph projected. Class identifies slope = g.

15–35 min

• Lab: pairs run 3 trials. Each trial: capture v-t, fit line to the falling portion, record slope. Take class average. Compare to 9.81.

35–40 min

• Sources of error discussion: detection angle, ball wobble, air resistance, sample rate. Which matters most?

40–43 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

43–48 min

title: Day 9 · Phase 2 — Projectile motion: two independent dimensions
bodyHtml:
DAY 9 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Gravity acts vertically only. Horizontal motion is unchanged.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K3. Projectile motion decomposes into independent horizontal and vertical components.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Vernier free-fall lab: measure g.

How today connects:

2026-XJ doesn't travel in a straight line — it curves under gravity. Projectile motion is the small-scale, local-gravity version of what an asteroid does at planetary scale.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Frame: "For the next three days, we explore curved paths under gravity. Everything we learn here scales up to orbits."

5–18 min

• Monkey-and-hunter sim or thought experiment. Drop a ball while pushing it sideways at the same instant a second ball drops from rest. They hit the ground at the SAME TIME. Why?

18–28 min

• Direct instruction: horizontal motion = constant velocity (vₓ stays vₓ). Vertical motion = free fall (vᵧ accelerates at -g). The two are INDEPENDENT. Vector decomposition refresher from Unit 1.

28–42 min

• Worked example: horizontal launch from a 5-m cliff at vₓ = 10 m/s. How long to hit ground? How far does it land? Walk through both calculations.

42–45 min

• Quick pair practice: 2 horizontal-launch problems.

45–48 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

48–50 min

• Marzano on K3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Ask students to compare two objects released from the same height with different horizontal speeds. Under the stated no-drag model, vertical motion and fall time are the same.

title: Day 10 · Phase 2 — Horizontal projectile launches

DAY 10 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Vary launch height + horizontal speed. Predict landing distance.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R2. Predict projectile landing given launch conditions.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Projectile motion: two independent dimensions.

How today connects:

Imagine 2026-XJ traveling horizontally past Earth at high speed. Does it strike? The answer depends on the BALANCE between horizontal speed and how much it falls during flyby. (Preview of orbits.)

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: yesterday's two-cliff problem. Anyone want to put it up?

5–15 min

• Direct instruction recap: vᵧ at time t = -g·t. y(t) = y₀ - ½g·t². x(t) = vₓ·t. Three equations on the board to reference.

15–35 min

• Group problem-solving rotation. 4 stations, 4-5 min each: vary cliff height (5, 20, 50, 100 m) and launch speed (5, 10, 20 m/s). Each group solves one, then rotates.

35–43 min

• PhET Projectile Motion: vary horizontal launch speed, watch landing distance change. Confirm group answers.

43–48 min

• Exit ticket: "From a 45-m cliff at 15 m/s horizontal, where does it land?"

48–50 min

• Marzano.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the order: use vertical motion to find time, then horizontal motion to find range. Students must use one shared time for both axes.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

TEACHER NOTES

title: Day 11 · Phase 2 — Angled projectile launches
bodyHtml:
DAY 11 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

v decomposes into vₓ = v cos θ and vᵧ = v sin θ. 45° gives max range on level ground.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R2. Full projectile reasoning, including angled launches.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Horizontal projectile launches.

How today connects:

2026-XJ doesn't approach Earth at 0° — it has SOME angle. Angled projectile math is what we'd use if it were going to enter the atmosphere.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Recap horizontal case. What's different about angled? (vᵧ ≠ 0 at launch.)

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: vₓ = v cos θ; vᵧ = v sin θ. Then the same vertical kinematics, but vᵧ starts positive instead of zero. Flight time uses vᵧ(end) = -vᵧ(start) for level ground.

18–32 min

• Worked example: 20 m/s at 30°. Compute vₓ, vᵧ, flight time, max height, range. Show every step.

32–42 min

• PhET sim: vary launch angle 0–90° at fixed speed. Class fills a table: angle vs. range. Pattern: 45° wins on level ground.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Why does 45° give max range on level ground? Reason it physically, not algebraically."

48–50 min

• Marzano on R2.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for correctly labeled initial components and a consistent vertical sign. The 45° maximum-range result requires equal launch and landing heights and negligible drag.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Differentiation: ELs — visual showing v decomposed at multiple angles; SWDs — pre-built sin/cos table for common angles; Honors extension — "what's the OPTIMAL angle to launch from a CLIFF? Greater or less than 45°?"

title: Day 12 · Phase 2 — Circular motion + centripetal force
bodyHtml:
DAY 12 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

a_c = v²/r. F_c = m v²/r. Always points toward the center.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S3. Compute centripetal force and acceleration for circular motion.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Angled projectile launches.

How today connects:

An orbit is circular motion. The force that keeps a satellite in orbit IS gravity, providing the centripetal force. Today we get the centripetal math; tomorrow we connect it to gravity.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: spin a ball on a string. Cut the string. Which direction does it go? (Tangent, not outward.) Why?

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: in circular motion, velocity changes DIRECTION even at constant SPEED. That's acceleration — toward the center. a_c = v²/r. The force that causes it: F_c = m v²/r. ALWAYS points inward.

18–32 min

• Worked example: a 1500-kg car rounding a 50-m radius curve at 20 m/s. What centripetal force does friction provide? Run the numbers.

32–42 min

• Worked example 2: satellite at 400-km altitude orbiting at 7700 m/s. What centripetal acceleration? Compare to g at that altitude. Notice: they MATCH. Tease orbit logic.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A ball on a 1-m string moves in a horizontal circle at 4 m/s. Mass 0.2 kg. What's the centripetal force?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on S3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that velocity is tangent to the circle and net force points inward. Students should name the interaction supplying the force rather than add an extra 'centripetal force.'

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: ball-on-string demo (with a stopper, not the actual ball, for safety); clear space; satellite altitude reference card.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 10 §10.3. Honors: Ch 10 §10.1–10.4 + Think and Solve 49, 53, 54.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §6.2 Centripetal Acceleration (pp. 249–252); §6.3 Centripetal Force (pp. 253–257). Focus: Explain inward acceleration and identify the real interaction supplying the centripetal force. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "string cuts → tangent": resist explaining. Ask: "What force was pulling the ball inward? When you cut the string, what happens to that force?"

Differentiation: ELs — pre-built free-body diagram with the centripetal arrow labeled; SWDs — equation written + units circled; Honors extension — "what if the car's speed doubled? How does the friction requirement change?"

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

title: Day 13 · Phase 2 — Newton's cannon: orbits as continuous falling
bodyHtml:
DAY 13 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Throw it fast enough, and the surface curves away as fast as the object falls.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K5. An orbit is continuous free fall around a body.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Circular motion + centripetal force.

How today connects:

2026-XJ has an orbit around the Sun. The Earth's orbit and 2026-XJ's orbit cross — or they don't. If they cross at the same TIME, that's the impact question. The framework for thinking about this is "orbits are falling."

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick recap centripetal force = mv²/r.

5–18 min

• Newton's cannon thought experiment. Cannon on a mountain, fires horizontally. Slow → falls into ground. Faster → falls further. Fast enough → falls AROUND the planet. That's an orbit.

18–30 min

• PhET Gravity and Orbits sim — vary satellite velocity. Slow = crash. Medium = circular orbit. Fast = elliptical, then escape. Class observes.

30–42 min

• Connect: for a CIRCULAR orbit, F_gravity = F_centripetal. Set GMm/r² = mv²/r. Solve for orbital speed v = √(GM/r). Compute for ISS altitude. (Should get ~7700 m/s, matching Day 12.)

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "In 2-3 sentences, explain why ISS doesn't fall straight down."

48–50 min

• Marzano on K5. Tomorrow: Kepler's laws.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for a curved free-fall path and an inward gravitational force. A successful explanation connects changing velocity direction to acceleration even at constant speed.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: PhET Gravity and Orbits on lab computers; Newton's cannon image or animation for the board.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 14 §14.1. Honors: Ch 14 §14.1–14.2 + Think and Solve 41, 42.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §6.6 Satellites and Kepler’s Laws: An Argument for Simplicity (pp. 269–271). Focus: Connect circular orbital motion with gravity. Use the class cannon model to explain continuous falling. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the cannon: "What happens if I fire it twice as fast as orbit speed? Three times?" (Elliptical, then escape — that's escape velocity. Foreshadow.)

Differentiation: ELs — visual of orbit as curved fall; SWDs — explicit derivation steps for v = √(GM/r); Honors extension — "what's escape velocity from Earth's surface?"

CPA teaching sequence: Start with a labeled sketch and a verbal prediction. Supply vector components and a center-to-center distance diagram before calculation; model one equation change per line, then use a parallel guided example and an individual check.

title: Day 14 · Phase 2 — Kepler's three laws
bodyHtml:
DAY 14 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Ellipses. Equal areas. T² ∝ r³. The constraints every orbit obeys.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K4. State and apply Kepler's three laws.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Newton's cannon: orbits as continuous falling.

How today connects:

If we know 2026-XJ's orbit shape and one period, Kepler's third law tells us EVERYTHING about its timing — including when it next crosses Earth's path.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: Kepler watched the stars BEFORE Newton invented calculus. He found patterns. Three of them.

5–15 min

• Law 1: Orbits are ellipses, with the central body at ONE FOCUS (not the center). Draw an ellipse on the board. Define foci, perihelion, aphelion.

15–24 min

• Law 2: Equal areas in equal times. Implication: orbits speed up at perihelion, slow at aphelion. Demo with a sketch.

24–35 min

• Law 3: T² ∝ r³ for objects orbiting the SAME central body. Show with Earth-Moon vs. ISS-Earth (same central body). Worked example: given semi-major axis, find period.

35–45 min

• Practice: use Kepler's third law to find orbital period for 3 different orbits around the Sun (Earth, Mars, an asteroid at a given semi-major axis).

45–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Write each of Kepler's three laws in one sentence in your own words."

48–50 min

• Marzano on K4.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that periods and semi-major axes refer to orbits about the same central body. Equal swept areas require greater speed near perihelion.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Ellipse drawing on the board (with foci marked); Kepler's-third-law worksheet with practice; semi-major axis values for Mars + a sample asteroid.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 14 §14.5. Honors: Ch 14 §14.3–14.5 + Think and Solve 47, 48.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §6.6 Satellites and Kepler’s Laws: An Argument for Simplicity (pp. 269–275). Focus: Distinguish Kepler's three laws and apply the period-radius relationship under the stated orbital assumptions. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on Law 2: after stating equal-areas, ask: "What does this say about the SPEED of the orbiting object near perihelion vs. aphelion?" Let them reason to "faster when close."

Differentiation: ELs — labeled ellipse diagram with all vocabulary on it; SWDs — Law 3 worksheet with steps numbered; Honors extension — "why does Law 3 only work for orbits around the SAME central body?"

title: Day 15 · Phase 2 — When does 2026-XJ arrive?
bodyHtml:
DAY 15 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Use Kepler + universal gravitation to compute 2026-XJ's closest approach and timing.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R4. Apply gravitation + orbits to predict closest approach (load-bearing for the unit).

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have used motion and force models to make an initial prediction for the fictional 2026-XJ. The next question is how gravity changes its path; a constant-velocity extrapolation is only a starting model. The preceding meeting focused on Kepler's three laws.

How today connects:

This is the day we answer the year-long question — at least for now — with the tools of Unit 2: where is 2026-XJ going to be, and when?

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Frame: "Today is the asteroid math day. We have the tools. We have the question."

5–18 min

• Class is given 2026-XJ orbital parameters: semi-major axis, eccentricity, current position. Walk through what each parameter means, on the board.

18–38 min

Group computation: calculate the orbital period and perihelion/aphelion distances from the supplied semi-major axis and eccentricity. Decide whether the orbit reaches Earth’s orbital radius. Separate that result from an Earth encounter: orientation, both bodies’ positions, timing, and uncertainty are also needed. Do not infer a collision date from orbital size alone.

38–43 min

• Compare today's prediction to Unit 1's prediction (which was just position-time extrapolation). What's different? Why is this one MORE trustworthy?

43–46 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

46–48 min

• Quick gather — who got what answer? Compare across groups. Discuss any discrepancies.

48–50 min

• Marzano on R4. Tomorrow: transfer task.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that students distinguish perihelion from distance to Earth. Orbital size and period alone do not establish an Earth encounter; orientation, timing, and uncertainty must be stated.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 14 §14.4, 14.6 + Think and Solve 40, 50.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §6.5 Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation (pp. 261–268); §6.6 Satellites and Kepler’s Laws: An Argument for Simplicity (pp. 269–275). Focus: Use orbit models to discuss what the given data constrain; orbital size alone does not establish an Earth-encounter date. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "why is this more trustworthy than Unit 1's?": push: "What assumption did Unit 1's prediction make? What do we know now that we didn't then?" (Unit 1 assumed constant velocity. Now we know acceleration depends on r.)

Differentiation: ELs — a labeled orbital diagram and quantity table; SWDs — a step-by-step calculation sheet; Honors extension — vary eccentricity by 0.01 and compare the perihelion distance. Explain why this sensitivity does not, by itself, determine closest approach to Earth.

Unit 2 Transfer Task Day 1: Receive, Plan, Begin

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

All Unit 2 targets, surfaced through transfer problems.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Use the evidence and supplied scenario data developed through this unit. Any new numerical data appear in the task itself; the asteroid remains fictional.

How today connects: Write a public-facing explanation of how gravity changes the 2026-XJ prediction, what the available data support, and what remains uncertain about an Earth encounter.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

Set the assessment conditions: individual work; calculator and the agreed equation/constants card allowed. Clarifying questions are welcome; physics-content coaching and new video help wait until after the assessment.

5–15 min

Read the task silently. Record what you notice and wonder. Clarify the meaning of the prompt and supplied data without discussing a solution.

15–25 min

Plan the work against Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Identify the needed diagrams, equations, evidence, units, assumptions, and public-facing explanation.

25–45 min

Begin the task independently. The teacher records approaches and access needs without giving content help.

45–50 min

Record the next step and the dimension that needs attention. Hand in work in progress for safekeeping; retrieve it at the next meeting. The task stays in class.

TRANSFER TASK

• Transfer task. Independent. 4 multi-part problems: (1) F_gravity Earth–asteroid + reasoning about how F changes at half the distance; (2) projectile launched at 25° from a 30-m cliff at 18 m/s — full kinematics; (3) ISS orbit altitude given orbit speed; (4) Kepler's third law on a Sun-orbiting asteroid given semi-major axis.

Public-facing transfer: Write a public-facing explanation of how gravity changes the 2026-XJ prediction, what the available data support, and what remains uncertain about an Earth encounter.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check the individual plan against all four rubric dimensions. Record equation choices, diagrams, and assumptions without supplying a method or correcting the assessment.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: transfer task printed; calculators; equation/constants reference card; quiet testing environment; growth chart pages.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: no reading.

Transfer task with all numerical data and assumptions; Unit 1 four-dimension rubric; permitted equation/constants card and calculator; planning sheet; a secure place to keep work between meetings.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: No new OpenStax reading during the transfer assessment. Use only the references permitted in the assessment plan; revisit a focused section after feedback.

TEACHER NOTES

Two-meeting assessment: This is the first of two full class periods. Day 17 is for completion, peer defense, final revision, and submission. The preceding synthesis lesson is retained.

Assessment conventions: Use the Unit 1 rubric: Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Score the four dimensions independently from 0–4; report the profile without averaging and use the established lowest-dimension conversion. Science checks the physics; Reasoning checks the choice and justification of the model; Communication checks labeled, organized work; Transfer-to-Asteroid checks the supported connection and its limits. Peer and student ratings are feedback; the teacher makes the final judgment. Target self-ratings use the separate 1–3 scale and do not automatically become mastery ratings. Revisions follow Unit 1’s two-week window, with new evidence for a one-level move on a dimension.

CPA access: Supply agreed labeled diagrams or vector components when component derivation is not the assessed target. Keep the same physics prompt and rubric; Honors students can justify or derive the corresponding model.

Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

40–48 min

Compare the self-rating with the evidence when giving feedback. Record the teacher’s judgments independently; peer agreement or completion is not a mastery score.

Work retained from the first meeting; the same task and permitted references; calculators; four-dimension rubric; peer-feedback sheet; final reflection and submission folder.
